20360-no-abolition-of-slavery-or-the-uni:
No Abolition of Slavery is a poem against ending the slave trade, cast as satire. In a stall three feet by four, a hump-backed cobbler drinks saloop. With him the muse shall sit and think, the poem declares. He shall complain, in sentimental strain, that negroes are oppressed.

The poem mocks such pity as false feeling in cheap print. Its title calls love's universal empire the true bar to abolition. Modern readers meet here the ugly case made for slavery in verse. The poem stands as evidence of the fight abolition had to win.
20804-lucretia-borgia-according-to-origi:
Old Roman houses still charm the historian in Lucretia Borgia, drawn from source papers. The Colonna, Orsini, and Gaetani families aided the work with open hands. Their aid let the writer test legend against records. Letters and lives could then speak for themselves.

Ferdinand Gregorovius sought the real Lucretia behind centuries of dark tales. Poison myths give way to a woman used by her family's vast plans. Rome, Ferrara, and the Borgia court fill the backdrop. The book counts as a model of history built from documents. It still shapes how readers judge Lucretia today.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PittsburghPostG:
Bob Hoover, the book editor of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, wrote this essay for the paper's Arts and Entertainment section. His subject is the rise of conspiracy thinking in American life. He opens with three investigated deaths: the playwright Christopher Marlowe, Lee Oswald, and Vincent Foster.

That opening trio does the essay's work. Suspicion, Hoover shows, is not new and not confined to one party or century. Marlowe's death was argued over in the 1590s; Foster's suicide in the 1990s drew the same machinery of doubt. The essay treats conspiracy as a habit of mind with a long history. It gives readers a newspaper editor's survey of why such stories spread and why they last.

nasa-tm-19630010644-design-analysis-of-a:
Six Lewis Research Center engineers wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-28. R. H. Cavicchi and H. H. Ellerbrock lead the author list. Their subject is a nuclear-powered cargo plane that flies below sound speed. Its reactor is cooled by helium gas, not water or air.

A nuclear plane could fly for weeks without refueling. That range suited heavy logistics work for the air force. The team worked out the design on paper, reactor and all. They weighed thrust, weight, shielding, and safety for the layout. The study dates to the bold years when atomic flight seemed near, and it shows the hard trade-offs that grounded the idea.
nasa-tm-19670005891-the-feasibility-of-a:
P. E. Schmid, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this study on September 1, 1966. It asks whether communication satellites of the 1970s could relay Apollo spacecraft data directly to a fixed station on Earth. Ground stations lost contact whenever a spacecraft passed beyond their horizon, leaving gaps in coverage.

Schmid considered relay satellites in 24-hour synchronous orbits and in lower 6-hour orbits. The relay would carry Unified S-Band ranging, telemetry, voice, and Doppler data, plus Apollo's VHF voice signal. The study found the main constraint was antenna pointing between the satellite and the Apollo capsule. Using omnidirectional antennas on both ends removed the pointing problem, though at a cost in signal strength. Feasibility, Schmid concludes, turns on how much antenna complexity is allowed.
nasa-tm-19670009725-tropospheric-and-ion:
E. Hirschmann, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in January 1967. It examines how two layers of air, the troposphere and the ionosphere, disturb radio communication. The work supported LOCAST, a project to locate aircraft by satellite transponder.

The paper's main purpose is a realistic estimate of the atmosphere's influence. Hirschmann focuses on errors in range and range-rate measurements. Those errors decide which operating frequency a system should choose. With the right frequency, a satellite at synchronous altitude could fix the position of a high-speed aircraft precisely. The introduction explains how signal deterioration arises in each layer.
nasa-tm-19670074061-postlaunch-report-fo:
Mission AS-201 gets its official reckoning in this postlaunch report, issued May 6, 1966, by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas. AS-201 flew Apollo Spacecraft 009. Postlaunch reports are the program's own record of what a mission did.

The front matter includes a table called Apollo Spacecraft Flight History. It lists the program's earlier tests in order. Pad abort and transonic abort tests at White Sands appear first, from late 1963. Nominal launch tests from Cape Kennedy follow through 1964. The table frames AS-201 as the next step in that test ladder. It stands as the flight's formal closing record, kept for later crews and engineers.
nasa-tm-19680027694-pulsational-instabil:
Norman R. Simon and Richard Stothers of the Institute for Space Studies at Goddard Space Flight Center study pulsating stars in this paper, part one of a series. Their subjects are massive blue stars with helium cores and thin, hydrogen-poor envelopes. Such stars can swell and shrink in regular pulsations, or stay stable.

Core structure barely changed when the hydrogen envelope was modified, they found. Total radius and luminosity did respond to envelope hydrogen content and gradient. Models stayed stable under modest central condensation conditions. Unstable models drew nearly all their energy from helium reactions in the core. Most damping happened in the thin non-burning hydrogen envelope. Pulsation periods stayed remarkably steady for each mass.
nasa-tm-19690011506-performance-of-an-ex:
Robert P. Macosko, William T. Hanna, Sol H. Gorland, and Kent S. Jefferies of Lewis Research Center report a long SNAP-8 power system test in this report. The experimental system ran for well over a thousand hours at Lewis. About eleven hundred hours of that running was continuous operation.

Steady-state performance did not degrade with time, the authors found. All prototype components performed satisfactorily except the parasitic load resistor, which failed during testing. Three automatic shutdowns occurred, and the protective system functioned properly each time. One erratic start flooded the mercury boiler with pressure and flow excursions. Even so, steady operation afterward was unaffected, and no oil contaminated the mercury loop.
nasa-tm-19710015102-the-potential-of-nuc:
G R Seikel and L D Nichols of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 propulsion meeting in Salt Lake City. It weighs nuclear MHD power systems for space and ground use. An MHD generator passes hot ionized gas through a magnetic field to make electricity directly. Very hot reactors make the idea attractive.

The study compared three power cycles built around such generators. A turbine assisted MHD cycle came out most attractive. It offered high efficiency with a modest radiator for space use. The authors also sized a large shielded space system. A ground station reaching about sixty percent efficiency also looked possible.
nasa-tm-19710028093-computer-program-for:
Lona M Howser and Stephen S Tompkins of the Langley Research Center documented a computer program for ablating bodies. An ablating body sheds its surface layer by layer under fierce heating, as a reentry heat shield does. Their program follows the time changing response of round symmetric bodies. It also tracks how the shape itself changes as material burns away. Earlier tools often froze the shape in place.

The report presents the program in full detail. Every subroutine and variable is listed and defined. Three worked sample problems show the printed and plotted output. That material helps a new user set up and run a case. The governing equation and solution method are also explained.
podcast-dannyjones-o5zBnkfDWpo:

Morton tells how he got inside closed lands and groups with a camera and a grin. He shares what North Korea felt like from the ground and what Scientology showed him. selections-from-american-poetry-with-spe:
Margaret Sprague Carhart edited this gathering of American verse, with special weight on Poe, Longfellow, Lowell, and Whittier. Contents begin with Anne Bradstreet's Contemplation and Michael Wigglesworth's Day of Doom. Colonial and early national voices lead the way.

Phillip Freneau, Francis Hopkinson, and Samuel Woodworth follow, with songs like Hail Columbia and The Old Oaken Bucket. Later pages center on the four named poets of the title. Teachers and students get a compact tour of American poetry from Puritan times onward, mixing famed pieces with lesser-known work from the young nation's first singers.
